name: The bark shed at Miller and Hall's tanyard

documented_range.note: NO SOURCE RECORD DATES THIS BUILDING, BECAUSE NO SOURCE RECORD NAMES IT. The bracket is the tanyard's own, carried across without being re-argued: `miller_tannery` - the log house Samuel Miller's brother John used as a tannery, with Benjamin Hall in from 1832 - carries 1831-01-01 to 1835-12-31, and a yard building that serves that tannery cannot honestly claim to have stood before it. Graded `reconstructed`, as the building is.

position.symbolic_location: On the point of land at the forks, in the yard behind John Miller's tannery, at the east end of the back row beside the drying shed, with its door facing south across the yard.
position.note:
INVENTED, AND SEATED BY THE WORKS RULE BELOW. THE TANYARD RUNS NORTH, BEHIND THE TANNERY, AND THAT IS WHERE THE GROUND IS. `miller_tannery` stands at bearing 180 with its face south toward Samuel Miller's house and tavern; behind it is north, on the point of land between the North Branch and the main stem. The two yard buildings stand side by side across that back yard, both with their front walls on one line at local N 83.200, which is 5.20 m north of the tannery's back wall - the cart yard figure T-1640 derived from `data/yard/town_trade_goods.json`. THE DRYING SHED TAKES THE INNER SEAT, its west wall on the tannery's own east wall line at local E 14.000, and THIS BUILDING STANDS BESIDE IT, 2.00 m further east at local E 18.438 to E 20.877. WHY IT IS EAST AND NOT AT THE WEST END OF THE YARD, which is where it was first drawn and which is the more obvious seat: the west end stands 67.86 m from the corridor it is nearest, and that is inside the EMPTY BAND `FRONTAGE_REACH_M` is cut from. `tools/measure_frontage_fabric.py` reads every building's distance to its nearest corridor, finds the body of that distribution continuous to 60.79 m and the next building anywhere at 74.65 m, and commits the midpoint of that 13.86 m gap - 67.72 m - as the reach beyond which a building fronts no street at all. A shed dropped into the middle of the gap does not break the town; it breaks the INSTRUMENT, by making the reach's own justification a 7.07 m band instead of a 13.86 m one, and the tool's self-test says so the moment it happens. An invented building is not a reason to move a committed constant, so the building moved: at this seat it stands 53.98 m out, inside the body of the distribution where 388 other buildings stand, and the band and the reach are exactly what they were. THE COST IS STATED: the two sheds no longer frame the yard from its two ends, they stand as a pair at one end of it, and the yard is open to the west. MEASURED ON THIS SEAT, over a 25 x 25 lattice on the placed polygon: the ground stands 1.141 m to 1.145 m above the committed water surface - dry, with 0.004 m of relief; `intrusion` reads it clear of all 33 platted corridors; the nearest committed footprint is the drying shed at 2.00 m and the tannery at 6.84 m. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: this is the best-placed of the four noxious trades - the tannery's own position is `inferred` on Andreas's 'just north of Miller's tavern' rather than reconstructed - so the SITE is about as good as this band gets and the BUILDING is still entirely invented. THE WORKS RULE BELOW. THE TANYARD RUNS NORTH, BEHIND THE TANNERY, AND THAT IS WHERE THE GROUND IS. `miller_tannery` stands at bearing 180 with its face south toward Samuel Miller's house and tavern; behind it is north, on the point of land between the North Branch and the main stem. The two yard buildings stand side by side across that back yard, both with their front walls on one line 5.20 m north of the tannery's north wall - the cart yard figure T-1640 derived from `data/yard/town_trade_goods.json` - and each with one wall on one of the tannery's own two side walls, so the yard is framed by the three buildings rather than scattered behind one. THIS BUILDING takes the WEST end: its east wall stands on local E 7.000, which is the tannery's own west wall line, and its front wall stands at local N 83.200. MEASURED ON THIS SEAT, over a 25 x 25 lattice on the placed polygon: the ground stands 1.129 m to 1.130 m above the committed water surface - dry, and flat to a millimetre, with 0.001 m of relief across the whole rectangle; `intrusion` reads it clear of all 33 platted corridors; and the nearest committed footprint is the tannery's own north wall at 5.20 m. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: this is the best-placed of the four noxious trades - the tannery's own position is `inferred` on Andreas's 'just north of Miller's tavern' rather than reconstructed - so the SITE is about as good as this band gets and the BUILDING is still entirely invented.

THE WORKS RULE, STATED ONCE AND APPLIED SIX TIMES (T-1709). Every one of the four documented noxious trades on the branches records, in its own footprint note, that the works are outside its polygon: `newberry_dole_slaughterhouse_south_branch` says 'the pens, the yard and the barrelling and salting space that a packing operation needs are outside the footprint and outside this archetype, which builds a building rather than a works'; `miller_tannery` says 'a tannery is its yard - bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply - and none of that is in this polygon or in the model'; `clybourn_slaughterhouse` says 'what is not modelled is arguably the bigger half'; `elston_soap_candle_manufactory` gives a shed 'big enough for a rendering kettle, a cooling and moulding floor and an ash leach' and nothing beside it. This building is one of the works those four sentences name, and NOTHING ATTESTS IT. It is placed by a rule and not by a plate. THE RULE: (1) a works building stands BEHIND its plant, on the side away from the water, because the plant's own bearing puts its working face on the water and the ground behind it is what is left; (2) the gap between the plant's wall and the works' wall is 5.20 m, the cart yard T-1640 derived from `data/yard/town_trade_goods.json` - 1.00 m of clearance from the wall a wagon stands at, plus the 3.20 m of ground a parked wagon needs, plus 1.00 m from the wall opposite - and the same 5.20 m separates one works building from the next, so the whole band is set out on one committed figure; (3) the works take the plant's own bearing, so the yard between them is square and the doors face it; (4) where the ground behind the plant is a platted street corridor, the works stand ALONG the bank instead, in the order the work runs, on a line that keeps them 0.50 m clear of that corridor's own edge - which is what the South Branch band does, because Market Street's corridor runs E 73.00 to E 97.00 at this reach and the plant itself stands 1.30 m inside it. THE FOUR PREDICATES each seat is held to, on a 25 x 25 lattice over the placed polygon: dry in the committed heightfield (`data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut`, WATER_SURFACE_M = 0), relief inside the 0.30 m `generate_block_infill.MAX_RELIEF_M` allows, clear of all 33 platted corridors (`tools/plat_corridors.intrusion`), and clear of every footprint the committed tree already places. docs/RESEARCH/branch_noxious_works.md carries the readings and docs/LIBERTIES.md L284 owns the invention.

derivation.reason: The two machine-checkable methods this project has are a platted corner and a traced waterline, and this seat is neither: it is a stated setback from a committed neighbouring building, on that building's own bearing, held clear of a committed corridor edge and tested against the committed heightfield. Every input is committed and the rule is written out in position.note, so it reproduces by hand; no derivation method in the schema can recompute it, and declaring one that could not would be worse than declaring none.

footprint.note: INVENTED. 2.4384 x 4.8768 m is 8 x 16 ft, inside family A4's band (6-8 ft front, 12-18 ft deep) - the crosswalk's woodshed and storage outbuilding. A bark shed is a store: hemlock or oak bark brought in, kept dry, and ground as it is wanted. The size is the family's and nothing states that this yard had a bark shed at all. Every number is invented.

construction.note: Notched logs, the archetype's `log`, because the building it serves is one - the sources call the tannery 'a log house ... that he used as a tannery' and this is the oldest of the four noxious sites, standing from 1831 on the point where the first log building in the settlement went up. At 2.44 m on its short side it clears the archetype's 2.2 m LOG_MIN_DIM_M, below which corner notching eats the wall. The fabric is reasoned from its neighbour and is not attested.

wall_height_m.note: About 7 ft 10 in, a shade over the archetype's size-aware default of 2.31 m for this plan. A man stands inside and forks bark; nothing here needs more. Invented.

roof_type.note: 4.88 m of depth is inside the 5.0 m at which `default_roof_type` gives a shed roof. Invented.

roof_pitch_deg.note: The archetype's default for a shed roof; the rise over this run is 1.59 m against a 2.4 m wall, inside SHED_RISE_RATIO_MAX. Invented.

door.note: 1.35 m clear - wide enough to barrow bark through, narrower than a wagon door, and it stands on a 2.44 m wall which carries it with a jamb either side. Invented.

door_side.note: The `front` elevation is the max-y wall, which at this bearing faces SOUTH, onto the yard between this shed and the tannery. Invented.

phases.change_note: One phase. This is a reconstruction of a works building the plant's own record says is missing, not a record of a building anybody named, so it has no history to divide into phases and inventing one would be inventing twice.

function.note: The closed vocabulary has no `bark shed`; `woodshed_or_storage_shed` is family A4's own name and a bark shed is a store. The specific use is in the record's NAME and in this note. The use comes from the tannery's own record, which says in as many words that 'a tannery is its yard - bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply - and none of that is in this polygon or in the model'. This is the first of those. No occupant is claimed.

part_of.note: This building was raised as the bark shed of John Miller's tannery, in the yard behind it, out of the tannery record's own sentence that 'a tannery is its yard'; it has no existence apart from that reading, so the tie is as reconstructed as the building (LIBERTIES.md L284, the works rule of T-1709). The tannery's keepers are seated on the tannery and are not repeated here.

research_note: A RECONSTRUCTED YARD BUILDING AT THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST FACTORY - T-1709, of T-1203. WHAT IS HELD: Andreas and DRLOIH for the tannery, its fabric, its year, its partner Benjamin Hall and its direction from Samuel Miller's tavern. WHAT IS INVENTED: this building and every attribute of it, including that it existed. WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED: the lime pits, the tan vats and the bark mill itself, which are pits and machinery rather than buildings - the tannery's record names them and this one does not discharge them. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE IT: any account of Miller and Hall's tanyard, or the Chicago Democrat's advertisements. Built under the owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18.
